newsitem.title: THAILAND: Major Thai crops hit by delayed rainfall.
newsitem.headline: Major Thai crops hit by delayed rainfall.

text.p: Major Thai crops including corn, soybean and sugar cane have been hard hit by an unseasonable dry spell which has damaged planting areas, government officials and industry sources said on Thursday.
More than 640,000 hectares of farm land in 22 provinces have already been affected by the prolonged dryness, according to deputy permanent secretary of agriculture Ananta Dalodom.
Thailand's rainy season normally starts in April or May, followed by a brief dry period in June, and it then resumes in July and August.
But this year, the dry spell in some areas, especially in parts of the north and northeastern regions, has been longer than usual, according to meteorological officials.
More than 70 percent of the first corn crop was damaged due to lack of rain during the crucial tasseling stage, causing a shortage of around 170,000 tonnes near-term, the industry sources said.
The commerce ministry is mulling whether to allow the local feed industry to import up to 150,000 tonnes of corn under a zero-tariff scheme to alleviate the shortage.
"Due to severe crop damage in certain areas, corn output might drop by 20 percent from its last projection," said Deputy Commerce Minister Chalermphol Sanitwongchai on Wednesday.
The agriculture ministry forecast in June that Thailand's 1997/98 corn production would reach 4.52 million tonnes.
Sugar cane has also been hit by bad weather.
The Cane and Sugar Board recently said that sugar cane output for the upcoming crushing season starting in November could fall 10 percent below target.
The Agriculture Ministry also recently advised farmers to delay planting their first rice crop to August instead of in the middle of July as usual.
The agriculture ministry's Ananta told Reuters that the ministry wanted to minimise damage that could be caused to crops by insufficient water.

"The slight delay will not affect production at all. Farmers should start planting when the amount of rainfall is sufficient and consistent since the first rice crop depends mostly on natural rain," he said.
But he downplayed the impact of the dry spell on crops.
"It is too early to say if we are facing drought this year. Rain could be late, but that might not mean drought," he said.

"When rains start falling regularly again, farmers can replant to make up for the damaged crops. In the case of rice, we can always compensate with the second crop if the first crop turns out to be lower than expected," he said.
If there was a drought this year, its magnitude would not be as bad as the one that struck Thailand in 1993 and laid to waste 2.56 million hectares of farm land, he added.
